title: Theory
content:
When a plano-convex lens of large radius of curvature is placed with its convex surface in contact with a plane glass plate, a thin air film is formed between them. This film has zero thickness at the point of contact and gradually increases in thickness outward toward the edges.

When this arrangement is illuminated with monochromatic light and viewed from above, interference occurs between light reflected from the bottom surface of the lens and the top surface of the glass plate. Since points of equal air-film thickness lie on circles centered on the point of contact, the interference pattern consists of concentric alternate bright and dark rings — these are called Newton's Rings.

Because thickness increases with radial distance, and path difference depends on thickness, rings crowd closer together as their order increases. This is why the diameter of a ring is not directly proportional to its order — instead, the square of the diameter (D²) is directly proportional to the ring number, which is the basis of the entire experiment.

The central spot of the pattern is dark rather than bright. This happens because light reflecting off the glass plate (a denser medium) undergoes a phase change of pi (equivalent to an extra half-wavelength path), while light reflecting off the curved lower surface of the lens does not. Even though the geometric path difference is zero at the center, this extra half-wavelength shift causes destructive interference there.
